doc.title: Adrian Cunningham interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 31, 2021

title: Playing well on a bad day: Brecker's advice
summary: Rowe and Cunningham discuss performing for the audience regardless of mood, and Cunningham relays Brecker's advice that your worst day must still be high.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Thanks for saying that. I have this personal feeling about when people think of jazz musicians often times they think they’re playing anything they want. They’re playing how they feel. And it seems that there are certain times when you’re on a gig and you © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
might feel crappy, but you’re playing for the audience. You can’t necessarily afford, I’m not even sure how to put this into words, to play how you’re feeling. You’ve got to play well.

Right. Yeah. Absolutely. It’s something I think about a lot, one of my Australian teachers studied with Brecker back in the day. And a great bit of advice he told me was that Brecker said to him, “Well what you have to work on is having your bad day, your worst day, at a certain level you know. Your best day could be up here, but your worst day can’t be lower, it has to still be up to a certain level, your worst day.” That’s what you’ve got to work on. And I think about that a lot. I think we have to, you know, our standard has to be so good that our worst day is still great. We have to work on playing our best and we have to work on our worst. That’s something I think about too. I think that’s really important.
